l: Tmolus mountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: The mountain of Tmolus stands steep and high, looking far over the sea, with Sardis on one side and little Hypæpæ on the other. Tmolus, the mountain's aged divinity, sits upon it to judge the musical contest.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Apollo and Neptune assume mortal forms and build the walls of Troy for Laomedon in exchange for an agreed payment. Laomedon refuses to pay and commits perjury, so Neptune inundates Troy and demands that Laomedon's daughter Hesione be exposed to a sea monster. Hercules rescues Hesione, but Laomedon also refuses Hercules the promised horses, leading Hercules to sack Troy. Telamon, who shares in the warfare, receives Hesione as his wife.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Apollo departs from Tmolus, assumes a mortal form with Neptune, and helps build Troy's walls for Laomedon in exchange for an agreed payment.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Neptune assumes a mortal form with Apollo and builds Troy's walls for Laomedon. After Laomedon refuses the promised reward, Neptune drives his waters toward Troy, inundates the land, overwhelms the fields, and demands Laomedon's daughter for a sea monster.

l: Laomedon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Laomedon is building the walls of Troy when Apollo and Neptune agree to complete them for a payment. After the work is finished, he refuses the reward and commits perjury; he later refuses Hercules the promised horses as well.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Troy is being enclosed by walls built by Apollo and Neptune for Laomedon. Neptune inundates the country after Laomedon's perjury, and Hercules later captures and plunders the city.

l: Hercules, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Hercules delivers Hesione from the sea monster and demands the horses Laomedon promised him. When Laomedon refuses the reward, Hercules captures and plunders Troy.

l: Hesione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Hesione, the daughter of Laomedon, is demanded for a sea monster and is chained to rugged rocks. Hercules delivers her, and she is later given in marriage to Telamon.

l: Telamon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Telamon shares in the warfare against Troy and receives Hesione as his wife.

l: Apollo and Neptune building Troy's walls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Apollo and Neptune assume mortal forms and build Troy's walls for Laomedon after agreeing on a payment in gold for the defenses.

l: Laomedon's refusal of the promised reward, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: After the walls are finished, Laomedon refuses the agreed reward, adding perjury to his false words. He later refuses Hercules the horses promised for rescuing Hesione.

l: Neptune's inundation of Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Neptune drives his waters toward Troy, turns the land into the form of the sea, carries off the wealth of the husbandmen, and overwhelms the fields with waves.

l: sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: The sea monster is the creature for which Laomedon's daughter is demanded as an appeasement to Neptune.

l: Hesione's exposure to the sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Hesione is exposed to the sea monster after Neptune's punishment of Troy and is chained to rugged rocks.

l: Hercules' rescue of Hesione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Hercules delivers Hesione from the sea monster and demands the horses that Laomedon promised as his reward.

l: Hercules' sack of Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: After Laomedon refuses the promised horses, Hercules captures the twice-perjured walls and plunders the conquered city of Troy.

l: Telamon's marriage to Hesione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Telamon, who shares in the warfare, receives Hesione and takes her as his wife.

l: Troy's walls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE IV. [XI.194-220]
s: Apollo and Neptune build Troy's walls for Laomedon in exchange for an agreed payment. Hercules later captures the walls after Laomedon refuses the promised rewards.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Proteus foretells that Thetis will bear a son greater in power and valor than his father, so Jupiter yields her to Peleus. Thetis assumes several forms to resist Peleus, but he follows Proteus's advice, holds her fast, and marries her; she bears Achilles. After Peleus kills Phocus and is exiled, Ceyx receives him in Trachyn and recounts how Dædalion became a hawk after Chione's death. Psamathe sends a wolf to avenge Phocus by attacking Peleus's herds, but Thetis intercedes and the wolf is turned to stone before Peleus is exiled again.

l: Proteus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Proteus foretells that Thetis will bear a son who surpasses his father in gallant deeds and is greater than him. He advises Peleus to bind Thetis while she sleeps and hold her through her transformations until she resumes her former shape.

l: Thetis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Thetis is foretold to bear a son greater than his father. She resists Peleus by changing into a bird, a tree, and a spotted tiger, but after he holds her fast she resumes her own form, marries him, and bears Achilles. She later intercedes with Psamathe on Peleus's behalf.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Achilles is born to Peleus and Thetis. He is the son foretold to surpass his father in power and valor.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Jupiter is in love with Thetis and is alarmed by the prophecy that her son will be greater than his father. He therefore avoids her embraces and has Peleus pursue her instead.

l: Peleus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Peleus seizes and restrains Thetis after following Proteus's advice, then marries her and becomes the father of Achilles. He is exiled for killing Phocus and seeks refuge with Ceyx in Trachyn. When Psamathe's wolf attacks his herds, he asks her to end the slaughter, and he later wanders to the Magnetes, where Acastus gives him an expiation.

l: Phocus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Phocus is killed by Peleus, an act that causes Peleus to be banished from his native home. His death leads Psamathe to send a wolf against Peleus's herds.

l: Ceyx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Ceyx, the son of Lucifer and ruler of Trachyn, receives the exiled Peleus with kindness. He tells Peleus how his brother Dædalion was transformed into a hawk after the death of Chione.

l: Dædalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Dædalion is described as active, warlike, and violent, unlike his peaceful brother Ceyx. After Chione's death, he grieves intensely, attempts to throw himself from Parnassus, and is transformed by Apollo into a hawk.

l: Chione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Chione, Dædalion's daughter, is highly beautiful and attracts many suitors. She bears Autolycus to Mercury and Philammon to Apollo, but Diana kills her with an arrow after Chione boasts that she is more beautiful than the Goddess.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Diana is offended when Chione prefers her own beauty to that of the Goddess. She shoots Chione through the tongue, causing her death.

l: Psamathe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Psamathe sends a wolf to avenge the death of Phocus and initially refuses Peleus's entreaties to stop it. After Thetis intercedes, Psamathe turns the wolf into stone.

l: Trachyn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Trachyn is the land and city ruled by Ceyx. It receives Peleus after he is banished for killing Phocus, although Peleus is later not permitted by the Fates to remain there.

l: wolf (Psamathe's avenging wolf), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: The wolf is sent by Psamathe to avenge Phocus's death. It attacks Peleus's herds with great fury, killing and mangling the cattle and some of the herdsmen until Psamathe turns it to stone.

l: marriage of Peleus and Thetis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: The marriage takes place after Peleus restrains Thetis despite her changing forms. It produces Achilles, and the text presents Peleus as happy in both his wife and his son, apart from his guilt over Phocus's death.

l: prophecy of Thetis's son, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Proteus's prophecy states that Thetis will bear a son who will surpass his father in gallant deeds and be called greater than him. The prophecy alarms Jupiter and causes him to yield Thetis to Peleus.

l: Peleus's killing of Phocus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Peleus's killing of Phocus is treated as his crime and causes his exile from his native home. The death also prompts Psamathe's vengeance through the attack of the wolf on Peleus's herds.

l: Chione's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Chione dies when Diana shoots her through the tongue for claiming superiority in beauty. Her death drives her father Dædalion into overwhelming grief and leads to his transformation into a hawk.

l: Dædalion's transformation into a hawk, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: After Chione's death, Dædalion tries to throw himself from the heights of Parnassus. Apollo pities him and gives him wings, a curved beak, crooked talons, his former courage, and greater strength in the form of a hawk.

l: hawk, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: The hawk was formerly Dædalion. It is hostile to other birds, attacks them without kindness, and becomes a source of grief to them while grieving itself.

l: wolf's attack on Peleus's herds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: The wolf emerges from a marsh near the sea and attacks Peleus's cattle with roaring fury. It kills and mangles the herd, wounds and kills some defenders, and leaves the shore and nearby waters red with blood.

l: wolf's petrification, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: After Thetis intercedes for Peleus, Psamathe changes the attacking wolf into marble while it is fastening on a mangled heifer. Its stone body retains the wolf's form but no longer has its color or power to cause fear.

l: Peleus's exile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: Peleus is banished from his native home for killing Phocus and seeks refuge in Trachyn. The Fates later prevent him from settling there, so he wanders to the Magnetes and receives an expiation from Acastus.

l: Thetis's transformations, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XI.221-409]
s: To escape Peleus's advances, Thetis changes successively into a bird, a large tree, and a spotted tiger. Peleus holds each form until she finally resumes her original form as Thetis.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: Ceyx prepares to undertake a voyage to Claros to consult the Clarian God about his brother’s fate, despite Halcyone’s fear of the sea. He leaves by ship, and after traveling some distance encounters a violent storm that overwhelms the vessel. The ship breaks apart and sinks, and many of the crew are drowned. Ceyx clings to wreckage, repeatedly calls for Halcyone, and is finally buried beneath a breaking wave.

l: Ceyx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: Ceyx decides to go to Claros to consult the Clarian oracle about his brother’s fate. He refuses to abandon the voyage or take Halcyone with him, promising to return before the moon has twice completed her orb. During the storm he thinks constantly of Halcyone, calls her name while swimming, and is finally submerged beneath a wave.

l: Halcyone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: Halcyone fears Ceyx’s voyage because of the dangers of the sea and begs him either to remain or to take her with him. She watches the ship depart until it disappears from sight, then returns to their bed in grief and anxiety.

l: the ship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: The ship leaves harbor with its oars, rigging, sails, and crew, but encounters increasingly violent winds and waves. Its seams open, water enters, the mast and helm break, and it is eventually sunk by the storm.

l: the sea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: The sea becomes white with swelling waves and is driven into violent upheaval by the winds. It rises toward the heavens, breaks against the ship, enters its hull, and finally engulfs the vessel and much of its crew.

l: storm, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: The storm grows during the night as fierce winds, rain, thunder, lightning, and enormous waves overwhelm the sailors’ efforts. It damages the ship, breaks its mast and helm, and drives a wave over Ceyx that buries him beneath the water.

l: voyage to Claros, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: Ceyx undertakes the voyage to Claros to consult the sacred oracle about his brother’s fate. The journey is cut short when the ship encounters the storm and is destroyed at sea.

l: the shipwreck, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: The shipwreck occurs after the storm tears open the ship’s seams, breaks its equipment, and sends it to the bottom. Many of the crew drown, while others seize broken pieces of the vessel; Ceyx clings to wreckage before being overwhelmed.

l: death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VII. [XI.410-748]
s: Death surrounds the crew as the storm destroys the ship, and many sailors are drowned. Ceyx’s final moments are spent calling for Halcyone before a wave covers his head and sinks him beneath the sea.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Halcyone, still unaware that her husband Ceyx has died in a shipwreck, prays to Juno for his safe return. Juno sends Iris to Sleep, who appoints Morpheus to appear to Halcyone in the form of dead Ceyx and reveal the truth. Halcyone discovers Ceyx’s body at the shore, mourns him, and is transformed with him into a bird. As kingfishers, they remain devoted to each other, and the sea is kept calm for seven winter days while Halcyone broods on her floating nest.

l: Halcyone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Halcyone waits for Ceyx, prepares garments for his return, and prays to Juno that he may be safe and prefer no other woman. After Morpheus reveals Ceyx’s death in a vision, she mourns, finds his body on the shore, and is transformed with him into a bird. As a kingfisher, she broods on a nest floating on the sea for seven calm winter days.

l: Ceyx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Ceyx dies when his ship is wrecked in the Ægean Sea. Morpheus appears to Halcyone in his form and tells her that the South wind shattered the ship and that he perished while calling her name. His body is later carried to the shore, where Halcyone finds it, and he is transformed with her into a bird.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Juno no longer endures Halcyone’s prayers on behalf of the dead Ceyx and seeks to remove Halcyone’s polluted hands from her altars. She commands Iris to order Sleep to send Halcyone a vision revealing Ceyx’s death.

l: Iris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Iris goes to the abode of Sleep at Juno’s command. She orders Sleep to send Halcyone a vision in the likeness of Ceyx and then departs along the rainbow after the vapour of Sleep begins to overcome her.

l: Sleep, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Sleep dwells in a dark, silent cave near the Cimmerians, surrounded by dreams and the waters of Lethe. At Iris’s request, he selects Morpheus from among his sons to carry out Juno’s command, then sinks back into drowsiness.

l: Morpheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Morpheus is skilled at imitating human forms, movements, faces, voices, clothing, and speech. Sleep sends him to Halcyone, and he assumes the form of Ceyx, appearing pale, wet, and shipwrecked as he tells her that Ceyx has died.

l: Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Through their pity, the Gods transform Ceyx and Halcyone into birds after Halcyone reaches his body and embraces him with her newly formed wings. Their transformation does not dissolve the couple’s conjugal love.

l: Trachyn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: Herculean Trachyn is the place where Halcyone is located when Morpheus’s vision, sent in the form of Ceyx, comes to her.

l: the Ægean Sea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The Ægean Sea is where the cloudy South wind catches Ceyx’s ship and dashes it to pieces. Ceyx’s shipwreck and death occur there.

l: the sea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The sea carries Ceyx’s corpse toward the shore, where Halcyone recognizes him. After the couple becomes birds, the sea remains calm for seven winter days while Halcyone broods on her floating nest.

l: the ship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The ship carrying Ceyx is caught by the South wind in the Ægean Sea and is shattered by powerful blasts and waves.

l: the shipwreck, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The shipwreck kills Ceyx and leaves his body drifting in the sea. Halcyone first learns of it through Morpheus’s vision and later confirms it when his corpse reaches the shore.

l: the vision of Ceyx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The vision of Ceyx is sent to Halcyone by Morpheus under Juno’s command. It appears as a pale, wet, grieving image of the dead Ceyx and tells Halcyone that he has perished in the shipwreck.

l: the transformation into birds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The transformation into birds occurs when the Gods pity Halcyone and Ceyx after she embraces his recovered body. Although they become birds, their love and conjugal bond remain intact.

l: the kingfisher, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, In the meantime, the daughter of Æolus, ignorant of so great
s: The kingfisher is the bird into which Halcyone and Ceyx are transformed. The kingfisher is associated with conjugal affection, and Halcyone is said to brood on a floating sea nest for seven calm winter days.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Æsacus, son of Priam and brother of Hector, falls in love with Hesperia, daughter of Cebrenus, while she is by her father’s stream. Hesperia is bitten by a serpent while fleeing him and dies, prompting Æsacus to throw himself into the sea. Tethys transforms him into a feathered didapper, but he repeatedly dives into the sea because he still desires death. The explanation notes that Apollodorus gives a different account, making Æsacus the son of Priam and Arisbe and attributing his transformation to grief over Sterope’s death.

l: Æsacus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Æsacus is presented as a son of Priam, brother of Hector, and descendant of Ilus, Assaracus, Ganymede, Laomedon, and Priam. He avoids cities and courts, falls in love with Hesperia, and pursues her until her flight leads to her death. In despair, he throws himself into the sea, is transformed into a didapper, and repeatedly dives in attempts to die.

l: Hesperia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Hesperia is the daughter of Cebrenus and is seen by Æsacus drying her hair beside her father’s stream. She flees from him like a frightened hind or water-duck, but a serpent bites her foot during the flight.

l: Hesperia's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Hesperia’s death occurs instantly after the serpent’s venom enters her body. Æsacus embraces her lifeless body, blames himself for pursuing her, and regards his own death as a necessary consolation for her fate.

l: the serpent, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: The serpent lies hidden in the grass and wounds Hesperia’s foot with its barbed sting while she is fleeing. Its venom causes her death.

l: the didapper, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: The didapper is a sea bird that cuts through the water with its legs drawn up and has a wide throat. Æsacus becomes one after Tethys prevents his attempted suicide, and its name is linked to its plunging into the sea.

l: Tethys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Tethys pities Æsacus as he falls from the rock and receives him softly. She covers him with feathers as he swims, preventing him from obtaining the death he seeks and enabling his transformation into a didapper.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Troy is represented through Æsacus’s royal ancestry and his connection with Priam and Hector. Priam is described as the one to whom the final days of Troy were allotted.

l: the sea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: The sea receives Æsacus when he hurls himself from a rock. After his transformation, he loves the sea and repeatedly plunges into it, while his feathers break his falls.

l: love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Love causes Æsacus to pursue Hesperia despite her flight. After Hesperia’s death, love contributes to his leanness and drives his repeated attempts to plunge into the sea and die.

l: Death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Death comes to Hesperia through the serpent’s bite. Æsacus seeks death in the sea after her loss, but Tethys prevents him from achieving it, leaving him condemned to continue living as a didapper.

l: the transformation of Æsacus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE VIII. [XI.749-795]
s: Æsacus is transformed into a feathered didapper after Tethys receives him in the sea. His new form has wings, a long neck, a distant head, and elongated spaces between the joints of his legs; he continues diving because the transformation does not satisfy his desire for death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The Greeks assemble at Aulis to sail against Troy after Paris brings Helen to the Trojans, but contrary winds delay them. Calchas interprets an omen of a serpent devouring eight birds and predicts a long war, then declares that Agamemnon must appease Diana by sacrificing Iphigenia; Diana substitutes a hind and allows the fleet to depart. After the Greeks land at Troy, Protesilaüs is killed by Hector, while Achilles fights and kills the invulnerable Cygnus. Neptune transforms Cygnus into a white swan, leaving only his armor behind.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The Greeks assemble at Aulis with a thousand ships and troops to avenge the rape of Helen and attack Troy. After Calchas's prophecy and the substitution of the hind for Iphigenia, they sail with favorable winds, land at Troy, and fight the Trojans.

l: Trojans, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The Trojans oppose the Greek landing and defend the shore. Their forces, including Cygnus and Hector, inflict heavy losses on the Greeks, although Achilles kills Cygnus.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Troy is the city against which the Greeks proceed after Paris brings Helen there. Calchas predicts that Troy will fall, though the war will last many years.

l: Paris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Paris brings Helen into his country, thereby bringing a prolonged war to Troy. His presence is absent from the offerings made at the tomb bearing the name of Æsacus.

l: Helen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Helen is the wife ravished and brought away by Paris. Her abduction prompts the Greeks to assemble and seek vengeance against Troy.

l: Agamemnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Agamemnon is the Greek king who must choose the public good over his affection for his daughter. Acting on Calchas's declaration, he permits Iphigenia to be led to the altar for sacrifice.

l: Calchas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Calchas, the son of Thestor and a soothsayer, interprets the omen of the serpent and the birds. He predicts Greek victory, the fall of Troy, and nine years of toil, and declares that Diana's anger must be appeased by the blood of a virgin.

l: Iphigenia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Iphigenia, the daughter of Agamemnon and a Mycenian maiden, is brought ready to offer her chaste blood at the altar. Diana spares her by placing a mist before the witnesses and substituting a hind in her place.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Diana delays the Greek fleet through her anger and requires the blood of a virgin to be appeased. When Iphigenia is offered, Diana substitutes a hind for the maiden, after which the winds become favorable.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Neptune is said by some to favor Troy because he made the city's walls. He is the father of Cygnus and transforms Cygnus's body into a white swan after Achilles defeats him.

l: Protesilaüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Protesilaüs is the first Greek to fall after the landing at Troy, killed by Hector's spear. His death fulfills the decrees of fate concerning the first Greek to land on the Trojan shore.

l: Hector, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Hector kills Protesilaüs during the defense of the Trojan shore. He is a formidable and initially unknown Trojan warrior, but Achilles is destined to face him only in the tenth year.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Achilles leads his chariot against the Trojan ranks and singles out Cygnus after seeking either Cygnus or Hector. Unable to wound Cygnus with spears, he attacks him with his sword and finally chokes him beneath his shield and knees.

l: Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Cygnus, the son of Neptune and a Trojan, kills a thousand men and proves invulnerable to Achilles's spears and sword. Achilles overcomes him by forcing him to the ground and tightening his helmet straps around his throat, after which Neptune transforms him into a white swan.

l: Euboean Aulis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Aulis is the Bœotian port where the Greek fleet is detained by contrary winds. It is the place where the Greeks witness the serpent-and-birds omen and where Iphigenia is brought to the altar.

l: serpent of Aulis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The serpent of Aulis, an azure-colored serpent, climbs a plane tree and devours eight young birds and their mother. It then becomes stone while retaining the form of a serpent.

l: hind substituted for Iphigenia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The hind substituted for Iphigenia is placed in her position at the altar when Diana casts a mist before the participants. Its death appeases Diana, allowing the Greek fleet to sail.

l: swan transformed from Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The swan transformed from Cygnus is created when Neptune changes Cygnus's body after Achilles defeats him. Achilles finds only the armor left behind.

l: Trojan War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The Trojan War begins after Paris brings Helen to Troy and the Greeks assemble to seek vengeance. Calchas's omen is interpreted as foretelling Greek victory and nine years of toil.

l: rape of Helen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The rape of Helen is the abduction of Helen by Paris from her husband, Menelaüs. It causes the Greeks to unite their forces and undertake the expedition against Troy.

l: sacrifice of Iphigenia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The sacrifice of Iphigenia is demanded by Calchas as the means of appeasing Diana and obtaining favorable winds. Iphigenia is led to the altar, but Diana substitutes a hind, so the maiden is not sacrificed.

l: Calchas's prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: Calchas's prophecy interprets the serpent devouring eight birds as a sign that the Greeks will conquer and Troy will fall. It assigns nine birds to the nine years of the war and states that the expedition's success requires the sacrifice of a virgin.

l: serpent-and-birds omen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The serpent-and-birds omen occurs at Aulis during a Greek sacrifice to Jupiter. An azure serpent devours eight birds and their mother, and Calchas interprets the event as predicting victory after nine years of war.

l: landing of the Greeks at Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The landing of the Greeks at Troy is opposed by the Trojans, who defend the shore. Protesilaüs is the first Greek to die, and fighting begins between the two forces.

l: death of Protesilaüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The death of Protesilaüs occurs when he is the first Greek to land on the Trojan shore and is killed by Hector. His death is presented as decreed by fate.

l: duel of Achilles and Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The duel of Achilles and Cygnus begins when Achilles singles out Cygnus after Cygnus has killed many Greeks. Achilles's weapons cannot wound Cygnus, but Achilles eventually throws him down and chokes him with the straps of his helmet.

l: transformation of Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE TWELFTH.
s: The transformation of Cygnus occurs after Achilles defeats him. Neptune changes his body into a white swan, leaving his armor behind.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: During a truce, the Grecian chiefs gather at a feast after Achilles defeats the invulnerable Cygnus. Nestor tells how Cænis, after Neptune’s assault, was transformed into Cæneus, a man who could not be wounded. At the wedding feast of Pirithoüs and Hippodame, the drunken Eurytus attacks the bride, provoking a battle between the Centaurs and Lapithæ. Cæneus survives countless blows but is finally crushed beneath piled-up tree trunks, after which Neptune changes his body into a bird.

l: Grecian chiefs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: The Grecian chiefs assemble during a truce at a feast held after Achilles’s victory over Cygnus. They discuss battles and marvel at Cygnus’s invulnerability, then listen to Nestor’s account of Cæneus.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Achilles defeats Cygnus and appeases Pallas with the blood of a heifer at a festive sacrifice. He asks Nestor to explain who Cæneus was, why Cænis changed sex, and whether Cæneus was ever defeated.

l: Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Cygnus is defeated by Achilles. His body can be pierced by no weapon and receives no wounds, astonishing the Grecian chiefs.

l: feast, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: A feast follows the truce between the Greeks and the Trojans, with the chiefs eating roasted flesh and drinking wine while discussing valor. The wedding feast of Pirithoüs and Hippodame later becomes the scene of violence when Eurytus attacks the bride.

l: Nestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Nestor tells the Grecian chiefs that he once saw Cæneus endure a thousand blows without injury. He recounts Cænis’s transformation, the battle at Pirithoüs’s wedding, and Cæneus’s death.

l: Cænis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Cænis is the beautiful daughter of Elatus and a Thessalian woman desired by many suitors. After Neptune violates her on a lonely shore, she asks him to make her no longer a woman and to protect her from suffering such violence again.

l: Cæneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Cæneus is the male form of Cænis and is famous for being invulnerable. He attends Pirithoüs’s wedding, withstands the Centaurs’ attacks, and is eventually crushed beneath tree trunks.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Neptune grants Cænis’s wish to become a man and additionally makes her unable to be pierced by wounds or killed by steel. After Cæneus’s death, Neptune changes his body into a bird.

l: Pirithoüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Pirithoüs, the son of Ixion, marries Hippodame and hosts the wedding feast attended by the Centaurs and Lapithæ. During the ensuing battle, he kills Petræus and is also credited with killing Lycus and Chromis.

l: Hippodame, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Hippodame is the bride of Pirithoüs and is praised for her beauty at the wedding feast. Eurytus seizes her by the hair, causing the conflict between the Centaurs and Lapithæ.

l: Centaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: The Centaurs are guests at Pirithoüs’s wedding feast. After Eurytus attacks Hippodame, they join the fighting, using banquet vessels and other objects as weapons; many are killed or wounded.

l: Lapithae, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: The Lapithæ attend Pirithoüs’s wedding and oppose the Centaurs after Hippodame is seized. Several Lapithæ are attacked or killed during the battle, including Celadon, Broteus, and Orius.

l: Theseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Theseus rebukes Eurytus for attacking Hippodame while Pirithoüs is alive. He takes Hippodame away from the attackers and kills or defeats several Centaurs during the battle.

l: Eurytus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Eurytus, described as the most savage of the Centaurs, becomes inflamed by wine and lust at the wedding feast. He seizes Hippodame, provoking Theseus and the battle between the Centaurs and Lapithæ.

l: Battle of the Centaurs and Lapithæ, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: The battle begins when Eurytus and the other Centaurs attack Hippodame and other women. Banquet objects, altars, torches, tree branches, and weapons are used in the fighting, and many Centaurs and Lapithæ are killed.

l: Cæneus's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Cænis asks Neptune to make her no longer a woman so that she cannot suffer a similar assault again. Neptune grants the request, and her voice becomes hoarser and seemingly male as she becomes Cæneus.

l: Cæneus's death and transformation into a bird, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: The Centaurs cannot wound Cæneus with their weapons, so they pile tree trunks upon him. The weight presses him to death, after which Neptune changes his body into a bird.

l: invulnerability, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XII.146-535]
s: Cygnus and Cæneus are presented as men whose bodies cannot be pierced or wounded by weapons. Cygnus’s invulnerability amazes the Grecian chiefs, while the Centaurs overcome Cæneus only by crushing him beneath tree trunks.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: During the Lapith–Centaur battle, Peleus kills several Centaurs, including Demoleon, Dorylas, Phæocomes, Chthonius, and Teleboas. Nestor recounts these combats and names other fighters, including Cyllarus and Hylonome, whose mutual love ends in their deaths. He then describes Cæneus resisting the attacks of the Centaurs until they bury him beneath a heap of trees. Mopsus says that Cæneus emerged from the pile as a tawny-winged bird, and the Lapiths continue fighting until many Centaurs are killed and the rest flee or are scattered by night.

l: Peleus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: Peleus sees Crantor grievously wounded by the pine hurled by Demoleon and avenges him by throwing an ashen lance through Demoleon’s ribs. He also helps fight the Centaurs, striking Dorylas after Dorylas’s hand is pinned to his forehead, and Nestor says that Peleus’s father knows how Nestor killed Phæocomes while Peleus was stripping the fallen enemy.

l: Nestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: Nestor narrates the fighting and claims to have killed or helped kill several Centaurs, including Phlegræus, Hyles, Hiphinoüs, Clanis, Dorylas, Phæocomes, Chthonius, and Teleboas. He says that he should have been sent to Troy, but that his age is now failing, and he recalls the deeds and names of many other warriors.

l: Cæneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: Cæneus fights the Centaur Latreus after Latreus mocks Cæneus as formerly a woman and urges him to take up women’s work instead of warfare. Cæneus’s body resists Latreus’s sword and the weapons of the other Centaurs; he ultimately remains beneath a pile of trees, after which Mopsus says that a tawny-winged bird emerged from the heap and identifies it as Cæneus.

l: Lapithae, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: The Lapiths fight the Centaurs in the Lapithæan house and continue using their weapons until some of the Centaurs are killed and the rest flee or are dispersed by night. Mopsus calls Cæneus the glory of the Lapithæan race.

l: Centaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: The Centaurs attack the Lapiths and include Demoleon, Dorylas, Phæocomes, Latreus, Monychus, Cyllarus, and others named by Nestor. They are repeatedly killed in combat, and their weapons cannot wound Cæneus; after burying him beneath trees, the surviving Centaurs are eventually killed, driven into flight, or scattered by night.

l: Battle of the Centaurs and Lapithæ, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: The battle involves close combat, javelins, swords, pikes, trees, stones, and other improvised weapons. Peleus, Nestor, Cæneus, and other Lapith fighters kill numerous Centaurs, while the Centaurs attack Cæneus collectively and bury him beneath a huge heap of trees. The fighting ends for the time being when some Centaurs are dead and the rest flee or are dispersed by night.

l: Cæneus's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: Latreus refers to Cæneus as having been born a woman and having received a reward that gave him the false resemblance of a man. The unit does not otherwise explain the transformation, but it presents Cæneus as a male warrior whose body cannot be wounded by the Centaurs’ weapons.

l: Cæneus's death and transformation into a bird, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, “Demoleon could not any longer endure Theseus enjoying this success in
s: The Centaurs bury Cæneus under trees until the weight covers his face and head and leaves him without air. Some say that the wood sent his body to Tartarus, but Mopsus sees a tawny-winged bird emerge from the pile and declares it to be Cæneus, once the greatest of men and now the only bird of its kind.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The unit explains that the Thessalians, especially those near Mount Pelion, were reputed to have pioneered riding and to have excelled in horsemanship. It interprets the Centaurs as possibly representing Thessalian or other northern horse-riding tribes, while also discussing several proposed explanations for their name and their alleged descent from Ixion and a cloud. The Centaurs’ conflict with Pirithoüs began over succession claims and was renewed when Eurytus, or Eurytion, attempted to seize Hippodamia at her wedding. After their battle with the Lapithæ, the Centaurs were driven from Thessaly toward Arcadia, Malea, and, according to some accounts, Italy.

l: Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Thessaly, especially the region near Mount Pelion, was said to be the place where horses were first trained for riding and used instead of chariots.

l: Thessalians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The Thessalians were reputed to have excelled all other Greeks in horsemanship, so that the terms for a horseman and a Thessalian became synonymous. Their skill in killing wild bulls was also associated with the name Hippocentaurs or Centaurs.

l: horsemanship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Horsemanship was said to have been perfected by the Thessalians, although one account considers the Lapithæ’s claim to have perfected it more probable. The discussion also suggests that Centaurs may have represented rude, horse-riding mountain tribes.

l: Hippocentaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The Thessalians acquired the name Hippocentaurs because of their skill as horsemen who hunted and killed wild bulls.

l: Centaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The Centaurs are variously explained as Thessalian horsemen, a rude northern race, or a rapacious people who ravaged neighboring country. They were said to descend from Centaurus, the son of Ixion, and were later portrayed as beings partly human and partly horse; after their defeat by the Lapithæ, they retreated through Arcadia toward Malea and, in some accounts, Italy.

l: Ixion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Ixion was said to be the father of Centaurus and Pirithoüs, the former by a cloud and the latter by Dia. The account suggests that the association of the Centaurs with Ixion may reflect the beginning of riding among the Thessalians during his reign.

l: Pirithoüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Pirithoüs was the son of Ixion by Dia and became the opponent of the Centaurs when they claimed a right to share in the succession to Ixion’s dominions. His wedding to Hippodamia was disrupted by Eurytus, or Eurytion, whose attempt on the bride led to the battle with the Centaurs.

l: Hippodamia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Hippodamia was the bride of Pirithoüs. The attempt of Eurytus, or Eurytion, on her at the wedding provoked the conflict between the Centaurs and the Lapithæ; one interpretation also proposes that she was a Centauress who married the prince of the Lapithæ.

l: Lapithae, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The Lapithæ are presented as a more civilized race that founded towns and gradually drove their wild neighbors, the Centaurs, into the mountains. They pursued the Centaurs after their battle and forced them toward the promontory of Malea.

l: Hippodamia's wedding, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: At Hippodamia’s wedding to Pirithoüs, Eurytus, or Eurytion, attempted to seize the bride. This incident led to the battle between the Centaurs and the Lapithæ.

l: war between the Centaurs and Pirithoüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The Centaurs declared war against Pirithoüs because they claimed, as descendants of Ixion, a right to share in the succession to his dominions. The quarrel was later reconciled, but renewed hostility followed the attempt on Hippodamia.

l: attempt on Hippodamia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: Eurytus, or Eurytion, attempted to seize Hippodamia, the bride of Pirithoüs. The attempt caused the consequences associated with the battle between the Centaurs and the Lapithæ.

l: Battle of the Centaurs and Lapithæ, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, EXPLANATION.
s: The battle followed Eurytus’s or Eurytion’s attempt on Hippodamia. Afterward, the Centaurs retreated to the mountains of Arcadia, and the pursuing Lapithæ drove them to the promontory of Malea in Laconia.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Periclymenus, brother of Nestor, transforms into an eagle while fighting Hercules, but Hercules wounds him with an arrow and kills him. Neptune mourns Periclymenus and asks Apollo to avenge him by secretly killing Achilles. Apollo directs Paris's arrow into Achilles, whose body is burned after his death, while his glory survives. Agamemnon then transfers the contest for Achilles' armor to the assembled Argive leaders, with Ajax, the son of Telamon, and Ulysses as the principal hopeful claimants.

l: Periclymenus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Periclymenus, the brother of Nestor and son of Neleus, possesses from Neptune the power to assume different shapes. In combat with Hercules, he changes into an eagle, but Hercules shoots him where the wing joins the side, and the arrow's continued pressure drives it into his neck.

l: Nestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Nestor relates the defeat of the Lapithae and Centaurs and is challenged by Tlepolemus for not mentioning Hercules's exploits. He explains that Hercules killed eleven of his brothers and Periclymenus, while declaring that he will not avenge them further by denying Hercules's brave deeds.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Neptune had granted Periclymenus the power to transform himself. He mourns Periclymenus after his death, resents Achilles, and asks Apollo to destroy Achilles with a secret arrow because Neptune cannot confront the enemy directly.

l: Hercules, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Hercules overthrows the walls of Messene and destroys Elis and Pylos. In battle with Periclymenus, he shoots the transformed eagle with an unerring arrow and kills him.

l: Hector, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Hector is described as an enemy whom the Greeks do not praise, despite his greatness. Apollo and Neptune recall Hector's death and the dragging of his ghost around Pergamus.

l: eagle (Periclymenus), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Periclymenus assumes the form of an eagle, using its wings, curved bill, and hooked talons to tear Hercules's face. Hercules wounds it in the joint between the wing and side, causing it to fall and die.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Apollo agrees to Neptune's request to avenge Periclymenus. Concealed in a cloud, he enters the Trojan army, tells Paris to aim at Achilles, and guides Paris's arrow so that it mortally wounds him.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Achilles is the fierce Greek warrior who continues to live after Hector's death and kills many Trojans. Apollo directs Paris's arrow against him, mortally wounding him in the heel, and his body is later burned; his glory nevertheless fills the world.

l: Paris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Paris scatters arrows among the less distinguished Greeks during the battle. Apollo directs him to aim at Achilles and guides his arrow to its fatal target.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: The Greeks defend Troy and suffer slaughter during the war. Paris wastes arrows on the vulgar Greeks before Apollo directs him to attack Achilles.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Troy's walls were built by Neptune and Apollo but are expected to fall. The city is defended through the deaths of many thousands, and Hector's ghost is recalled as having been dragged around Pergamus.

l: arrow (Apollo's), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Apollo directs Paris's unerring arrow toward Achilles with a fatal right hand. The arrow mortally wounds Achilles in the heel, described as the only vulnerable part of his body.

l: Agamemnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Agamemnon, the descendant of Tantalus, refuses to decide the dispute over Achilles' armor by himself. He orders the Argive leaders to judge the contest together in the camp.

l: Ulysses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Ulysses, the son of Laertes, is named as one of the two principal figures who might claim Achilles' armor. The text presents him as a stronger prospect than the other listed challengers.

l: the arms of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Achilles' armor becomes the cause of a dispute after Achilles's death. The arms are taken up against one another in a contest, chiefly involving the son of Telamon and Ulysses, while Agamemnon assigns the decision to the Argive leaders.

l: death of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: Achilles's death is caused when Apollo directs Paris's arrow into his heel, his only vulnerable part. His body is then burned, leaving little ash, but his glory survives and is said to fill the whole world.

l: the contest for Achilles’ arms, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XII.536-628]
s: After Achilles dies, his armor prompts a dispute among the Greek leaders. Agamemnon transfers judgment of the contest to the assembled Argive leaders, with the son of Telamon and Ulysses presented as the main hopeful claimants.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: After Achilles’ death, Ajax and Ulysses contend before the Greek chiefs for Achilles’ armour. Ajax argues that his strength, lineage, and defense of the Grecian fleet make him more deserving than Ulysses, whom he accuses of cowardice, deceit, and abandoning wounded comrades. He recounts defeating Hector and protecting Diomedes, and challenges Ulysses to retrieve the arms from the enemy. The contest ultimately results in Ulysses receiving the armour, after which Ajax kills himself and his blood is changed into a flower; Ulysses later brings Philoctetes to the siege of Troy, and Troy falls.

l: Ajax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Ajax, described as the lord of the seven-fold shield, argues before the Greek chiefs that his lineage, courage, and deeds in battle entitle him to Achilles’ arms. He says that he defended the Grecian fleet, protected Diomedes, and defeated Hector, while accusing Ulysses of cowardice and deceit. After the armour is awarded to Ulysses, Ajax kills himself, and his blood is changed into a flower.

l: Ulysses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Ulysses contends with Ajax for Achilles’ arms. Ajax accuses him of avoiding war by feigning madness, engineering Palamedes’ death, abandoning Nestor, and relying on stealth and eloquence rather than open combat. Ulysses receives the armour and later brings Philoctetes to the siege of Troy.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Achilles is dead, and Ajax and Ulysses contend for the armour that belonged to him. Ajax emphasizes that Achilles was his cousin and argues that this relationship supports his claim to the arms.

l: Hector, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Hector brings fire and sword against the Grecian fleet and is accompanied by the Gods in battle. Ajax says that he faced Hector in close combat, struck him down with a huge stone, and was not defeated by him.

l: Philoctetes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Philoctetes, the son of Pœas, is left exposed on Lemnos through the Greeks’ actions. He is described as living in sylvan caves, suffering from disease and famine, and using Hercules’ arrows to shoot birds. Ulysses later brings him to the siege of Troy.

l: Grecian chiefs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The Greek chiefs sit in judgment while Ajax and Ulysses contend for Achilles’ armour. They adjudge the armour to Ulysses.

l: Pelasgians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The Greeks witness Ajax’s deeds and are addressed by him during the contest. They had prayed that Ajax would face Hector, and they previously left Philoctetes on Lemnos and accepted Ulysses’ accusations against Palamedes.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Troy is besieged after Ulysses brings Philoctetes, whose possession of Hercules’ arrows helps fulfill the destinies of Troy. Troy is then taken and sacked, and Hecuba becomes the slave of Ulysses.

l: Grecian fleet, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The Grecian fleet is threatened by the Trojans’ fire and sword and by Jupiter. Ajax claims that he protected its thousand ships with his own body.

l: the arms of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The arms of Achilles are the object of the contest between Ajax and Ulysses. Ajax argues that they should belong to him because of his kinship with Achilles and his battlefield service, but the Greek chiefs award them to Ulysses.

l: seven-fold shield of Ajax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: Ajax is identified as the lord of the seven-fold shield. He says that his shield protected Diomedes and that he used it to defend the Grecian fleet.

l: arrows of Hercules, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The arrows of Hercules are possessed by Philoctetes. Although Philoctetes is suffering on Lemnos, he uses the arrows to shoot birds; they are later brought to the siege of Troy and help accomplish Troy’s destined destruction.

l: the contest for Achilles’ arms, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The contest for Achilles’ armour is argued before the Greek chiefs by Ajax and Ulysses. Ajax bases his claim on his lineage, courage, and service, while attacking Ulysses’ reliance on speech and stratagem; the armour is awarded to Ulysses.

l: Trojan War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, BOOK THE THIRTEENTH.
s: The siege of Troy continues until Ulysses brings Philoctetes and the arrows of Hercules, allowing the destinies of Troy to be accomplished. Troy is subsequently taken and sacked.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Ulysses argues before the Greek chiefs that he deserves Achilles’ arms because his counsel and daring enabled many Greek successes in the Trojan War. He recounts discovering Achilles in disguise, recovering Philoctetes, killing Dolon and Rhesus, carrying Achilles’ body, entering Troy to seize the statue of Minerva, and performing other services. Ajax is portrayed as strong but lacking intelligence, while Ulysses claims that wisdom has made Troy capable of being captured. The chiefs award the arms to Ulysses, and Ajax, overcome by anger and grief, kills himself with his sword; from his blood a purple flower grows.

l: Ajax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Ajax contends with Ulysses for the arms of Achilles. Ulysses depicts him as a powerful but unintelligent fighter who has few wounds and relies on physical strength, and the chiefs award the arms to Ulysses instead.

l: Ulysses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Ulysses delivers the successful speech for Achilles’ arms, claiming credit for numerous acts of counsel, diplomacy, reconnaissance, and combat during the Trojan War. He says that he discovered Achilles in disguise, brought the Greeks back from flight, killed Dolon and Rhesus, carried Achilles’ body, entered Troy to seize the statue of Minerva, and made Troy capable of being conquered.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Achilles is the dead hero whose arms are disputed by Ajax and Ulysses. Ulysses claims that he found Achilles disguised as a maiden and sent him to war, later carried his body and arms from the battlefield, and now seeks to receive those arms.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: The Greeks hear Ulysses’ account of his services and are urged to acknowledge his wisdom and labor. Their chiefs are moved by his eloquence and award him Achilles’ arms.

l: the arms of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: The arms of Achilles are contested by Ajax and Ulysses after Achilles’ death. Ulysses argues that he deserves them because he discovered Achilles, carried his body and arms, and helped make Troy conquerable; the chiefs give them to Ulysses.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Troy resists the Greeks throughout the long war, but Ulysses claims that his actions, especially the capture of the statue of Minerva, made it capable of being taken. He says that he entered its walls and highest towers and removed the statue from its shrine.

l: the statue of Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Ulysses says that he carried the hidden statue of Minerva away from the middle of the enemy. He reveals the statue before the chiefs as a final appeal, asserting that Troy could not be captured without it.

l: Trojan War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: The Trojan War has lasted ten years when Ulysses recounts his services in it. He describes advising the Greeks, conducting missions and ambushes, recovering allies, resisting their attempted departure, and carrying out dangerous actions against the Trojans.

l: the contest for Achilles’ arms, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: The contest is between Ajax and Ulysses, with descent, personal merit, and service proposed as grounds for the decision. Ulysses wins the contest through his speech, and the chiefs give him Achilles’ arms.

l: Ulysses’ speech, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: Ulysses’ speech presents him as the chief source of Greek victories through intelligence, eloquence, and daring rather than physical strength alone. Its eloquence moves the chiefs, who award him the arms of Achilles.

l: Ajax’s suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The son of Telamon had {now} ended, and a murmur among the multitude
s: After Ulysses receives Achilles’ arms, Ajax is overcome by anger and grief. He declares that his sword is still his own, plunges it into his breast, and dies; his blood causes a purple flower to grow from the earth.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: After Ulysses recovered the arrows of Hercules with their owner’s help, the Greeks finally completed the long Trojan War and Troy fell. Priam was killed at Jupiter’s altar, Hecuba was carried away after mourning Hector’s ashes, Cassandra was dragged away, and Astyanax was hurled from the towers. The text then recounts how Polydorus, entrusted to Polymnestor in Thrace, was murdered for the sake of his riches. The explanation also discusses the rivalry of Ajax Telamon and Ulysses over the armour of Achilles and the related Palladium dispute.

l: Ulysses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Ulysses sailed to Lemnos, the country of Hypsipyle, to recover the arrows of Hercules, and returned them to the Greeks with their owner attending. His actions helped bring the protracted Trojan War to an end, and the explanation describes his rivalry with Ajax Telamon over the armour of Achilles and, in some accounts, the Palladium.

l: Ajax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Ajax Telamon is presented in the explanation as Ulysses’ rival in the dispute over the armour of Achilles. After losing the award in the more general account, he became distracted, attacked flocks that he mistook for enemies, and eventually stabbed himself with Hector’s sword.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: After receiving the recovered arrows, the Greeks completed the war and destroyed Troy. They dragged away the Dardanian matrons, including Hecuba, while taking the statues of their gods and the treasures of the burning temples.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Troy and Priam fell together after the recovered arrows enabled the Greeks to finish the war. Ilion burned near the narrowed Hellespont, while its temples, towers, and royal household were destroyed.

l: Priam, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Priam was killed at the altar of Jupiter, where the scanty blood of the aged king was consumed by the flames.

l: Hecuba, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Hecuba was found among the sepulchres of her children and dragged away by Dulichian hands. Before leaving, she mourned at the tombs, took Hector’s ashes in her bosom, and left her grey hair and tears on his tomb.

l: Hector, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Hecuba carried Hector’s ashes away from Troy and left an offering of her hair and tears on his tomb. The explanation also says that Hector’s body was dragged around Troy by the belt he had received from Ajax Telamon.

l: Polydorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Polydorus was entrusted by his father to Polymnestor to be raised secretly away from the Phrygian arms. When the Phrygian fortunes were ruined, Polymnestor murdered him and threw his lifeless body from a rock into the waters below.

l: Polymnestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Polymnestor was the king of the Bistonians in Thrace and kept the rich palace where Polydorus was sent to be raised. He murdered Polydorus for the riches entrusted with him and cast the body into the water.

l: Thrace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Thrace is described as the foreign land opposite Phrygia, where Troy had stood. It was inhabited by the Bistonians and contained Polymnestor’s palace.

l: Agamemnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Agamemnon is identified as the commander to whom Cassandra became captive after being ravished by Ajax Oïleus. The explanation also says that he adjudicated the dispute between Ajax Telamon and Ulysses, consulting Trojan prisoners and spies before deciding in favour of Ulysses.

l: Diomedes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Diomedes is described as Ulysses’ constant companion in several exploits. Together with Ulysses, he captured Helenus and killed Rhesus and Dolon, and he rescued Nestor when Ulysses had fled.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: Achilles is connected with the armour over which Ajax Telamon and Ulysses disputed. The explanation also says that Achilles had been concealed in female apparel at the court of Lycomedes, where he married Deidamia and fathered Pyrrhus.

l: the statue of Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: The Palladium was the hidden statue of Minerva that was believed to guard Troy’s safety while it remained in Trojan possession. Some ancient writers said that the dispute between Ajax Telamon and Ulysses concerned which of them should possess it.

l: Palladium dispute, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: According to Dictys, Suidas, and Cedrenus, Ajax Telamon and Ulysses disputed possession of the Palladium, and the Grecian nobles awarded it to Ulysses. Other accounts instead make the dispute concern the armour of Achilles.

l: Trojan War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: The Trojan War is described as a protracted conflict that ended after Ulysses brought back the arrows of Hercules with their owner’s help. Its conclusion led to the fall and burning of Troy and the enslavement of the Trojan women.

l: capture and sack of Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: The fall of Troy involved the destruction of Ilion, the death of Priam, the enslavement of the Dardanian matrons, and the burning of the city’s roofs and temples. Astyanax was thrown from the towers, and Hecuba was carried away after mourning the dead.

l: story of Polydorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: The story of Polydorus concerns his being sent by Priam to Polymnestor for secret upbringing, followed by his murder when the fortunes of the Phrygians collapsed. The explanation adds that, in another version, Ilione secretly raised Polydorus as her own son, Polymnestor accidentally killed his own son Deiphylus, and Polydorus later learned the truth and deprived Polymnestor of sight.

l: armour of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The conqueror, Ulysses, set sail for the country of Hypsipyle,[48] and
s: The armour of Achilles was the object of the rivalry between Ajax Telamon and Ulysses in the account most generally followed by the text. After Ulysses obtained it, Ajax became distraught and killed himself with the sword Hector had given him.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: After the Greeks moor in Thrace, Achilles' ghost demands that Polyxena be sacrificed at his tomb, and Neoptolemus kills her despite her courage and pleas for modest treatment. Hecuba, grieving over Polyxena, discovers the murdered body of Polydorus, takes revenge on Polymnestor by blinding him, and is transformed into a bitch. Aurora mourns her son Memnon, whom Achilles killed, and Jupiter transforms the ashes from Memnon's funeral pyre into the fighting birds called Memnonides.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The Greeks moor their fleet on the Thracian shore while waiting for calmer seas and more favorable winds. They obey Achilles' ghost and allow Polyxena to be sacrificed.

l: Thrace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Thrace is where the Greeks halt on their return from Troy. Its people attack Hecuba with darts and stones after she blinds Polymnestor.

l: Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Achilles' ghost rises from the ground and demands that Polyxena be sacrificed to appease his spirit. He had killed Memnon, and Hecuba calls him the ruin of Troy and the destroyer of many of her children.

l: Polyxena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Polyxena is led from Hecuba to Achilles' tomb and sacrificed by Neoptolemus. She faces death courageously, asks that her body be returned unburned to her mother, and preserves her modesty as she falls.

l: Hecuba, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Hecuba mourns Polyxena, discovers Polydorus's murdered body, and takes revenge on Polymnestor. After the Thracians attack her, she barks and is transformed into a bitch.

l: Agamemnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Agamemnon is identified as the son of Atreus, whose fleet is moored on the Thracian shore. Achilles had previously attacked him with his sword.

l: Priam, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Priam is remembered as Hecuba's husband and as the king whose house loses Troy and its children. Hecuba says that he was fortunate to die before seeing Polyxena cut off.

l: Polydorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Polydorus, Hecuba's youngest surviving male child, had been entrusted to the Ismarian king. Hecuba finds his corpse on the shore, bearing great wounds inflicted by Thracian weapons.

l: Polymnestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Polymnestor, the Odrysian king, murders Polydorus and is lured by Hecuba with the promise of a hidden treasure. Hecuba and the captive Trojan matrons attack him, tear out his eyes, and leave the sockets empty.

l: Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Troy lies prostrate after its destruction, and Hecuba describes its fall as the public calamity of her family. The text also calls Achilles the ruin of Troy.

l: Trojans, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The Trojan matrons receive Polyxena's body and mourn the bloodshed suffered by Priam's house. They accompany Hecuba in her grief and help her attack Polymnestor.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Jupiter grants Aurora's request to honor Memnon after his death. At his assent, the ashes from Memnon's funeral pyre become birds.

l: Aurora, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Aurora mourns her son Memnon, whom she saw Achilles kill, and asks Jupiter to give him an honor that will console her. She continues to shed tears of affection as dew over the world.

l: Memnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Memnon is killed by Achilles on the Phrygian plains while fighting for his uncle. His funeral pyre becomes the source of the Memnonides after Aurora asks Jupiter to ease her grief.

l: Memnonides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The Memnonides arise from the ashes and embers of Memnon's funeral pyre. They divide into two opposing groups, fight with beaks and claws, and are destined to perish in battle each year in honor of their parent.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The sacrifice of Polyxena is demanded by Achilles' ghost as an offering for his tomb. Neoptolemus performs it, and Polyxena dies while asking that her body be returned to Hecuba.

l: Hecuba's transformation into a bitch, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Hecuba's transformation into a bitch follows her revenge against Polymnestor and the attack by the Thracian people. Her mouth becomes suited to barking, and she howls through the Sithonian plains.

l: funeral of Memnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The funeral of Memnon includes a lofty pyre whose fires sink after Jupiter grants Aurora's request. Its smoke, embers, and ashes gather into living birds that become the Memnonides.

l: tomb of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: The tomb of Achilles is the place where Polyxena is sacrificed to appease his ghost. Hecuba says that Achilles remains an enemy of her family even from his tomb.

l: Achilles' ghost, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Achilles' ghost rises before the Greeks and reproaches them for leaving without remembering his valor. It demands that Polyxena be slain so that his sepulchre will not lack honor.

l: Hecuba's revenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES III. AND IV. [XIII.439-622]
s: Hecuba's revenge begins when she discovers that Polymnestor has murdered Polydorus. She falsely promises him a hidden treasure, then attacks him with the captive matrons and tears out his eyes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: After the fall of Troy, Æneas travels with Anchises and Ascanius to Delos, where Anius receives them and recounts how his daughters were transformed into doves by Bacchus. Apollo’s oracle directs the Trojans to seek the ancient mother and kindred shores, and Anius gives them gifts before their departure. The account also describes the daughters of Orion, who sacrifice themselves to save Thebes from a plague, after which two youths arise from their ashes and are called Coronae. Æneas’s voyage then passes Ambracia and Dodona, whose traditions include divine disputes, transformations, and an ancient oracle.

l: Æneas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Æneas escapes the ruins of Troy carrying the sacred relics and Anchises, and travels with Ascanius by sea to Delos. He is received by Anius, consults Apollo’s oracle, receives a goblet from Anius, and gives gifts in return before continuing his voyage toward the Ausonian shores.

l: Anchises, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Anchises escapes Troy on Æneas’s shoulders and accompanies him to Delos. He recognizes Anius and asks about Anius’s son and four daughters, and he receives a sceptre from Anius at the Trojans’ departure.

l: Ascanius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Ascanius escapes Troy with Æneas and Anchises and travels with them to Delos. Anius gives him a scarf and a quiver before the Trojans depart.

l: Anius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Anius is king of Delos and priest of Apollo. He receives Æneas, Anchises, and Ascanius into his temple and house, recounts the fate of his daughters, consults Apollo’s oracle with them, and gives gifts to the departing Trojans.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Apollo is the god served by Anius at Delos. His oracle directs the Trojans to seek the ancient mother and the kindred shores, and Apollo is also associated with Ambracia, where a temple is later renowned as the Actian Apollo.

l: Anius’s daughters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
s: Anius’s daughters received gifts from Liber that enabled them to transform things into corn, wine, and the berry of Minerva. The son of Atreus compelled them to provision the Argive fleet; after they sought help from Bacchus, they lost their human forms and became snow-white doves.

l: doves of Cytherea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLES V. AND VI. [XIII.623-718]
